facts.title: The Lazy Gas
facts.text: Argon's name comes from the Greek word "argos," meaning "lazy" or "idle," a nod to its extreme chemical unreactivity. Like the other noble gases, its outer electron shell is completely full (electron configuration [Ne]3s²3p⁶), so it has almost no drive to bond with other atoms. For over a century chemists believed it formed no compounds at all.

facts.title: Discovered by Subtraction
facts.text: In 1894, Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay noticed that nitrogen extracted from air was about 0.5% denser than nitrogen made chemically. By removing the oxygen, nitrogen, and other known gases from air, they isolated a mysterious leftover gas — argon. The discovery earned Rayleigh the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics and Ramsay the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

facts.title: The Third Most Common Air
facts.text: Argon makes up about 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere by volume, making it the third most abundant atmospheric gas after nitrogen and oxygen. That means there is far more argon in the air you breathe than carbon dioxide. It is also the most abundant noble gas on Earth by a wide margin.

facts.title: Born From Radioactive Decay
facts.text: Most of Earth's argon is argon-40, and almost all of it formed underground from the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks over billions of years. This is why argon is so common in our atmosphere compared to the cosmos at large. Geologists exploit this in potassium-argon dating to measure the age of volcanic rocks and ancient minerals.

facts.title: A Different Argon in Space
facts.text: In the universe as a whole, the dominant isotope is argon-36, produced by nuclear fusion in massive stars, not the argon-40 that dominates on Earth. Argon is actually one of the more common elements in the cosmos. In 2013 the Herschel Space Observatory detected argon hydride (ArH⁺) in the Crab Nebula — the first noble-gas molecule ever found in space.

facts.title: It Can Form Compounds After All
facts.text: For decades argon was thought to be completely inert, but in 2000 a team at the University of Helsinki created argon fluorohydride (HArF). The molecule is only stable at temperatures below about 27 kelvin (−246 °C), but its existence proved argon chemistry is possible. It remains the only neutral argon compound ever synthesized.

facts.title: Shielding the Welder's Arc
facts.text: Argon's reluctance to react makes it a perfect protective blanket. In TIG and MIG welding it is blown over the molten metal to shield it from oxygen and nitrogen, which would otherwise weaken the weld. The same inert quality lets it fill the space inside double-glazed windows, where it insulates better than ordinary air.

facts.title: Glowing Lilac in a Tube
facts.text: When electricity is passed through low-pressure argon, it glows a distinctive lilac or pale violet-blue. This makes it a workhorse in lighting and neon-style signs, and it was once used to fill incandescent bulbs to stop the tungsten filament from burning up. Argon is also the buffer gas in many fluorescent lamps and plasma displays.

facts.title: Preserving the Past
facts.text: Because it crowds out reactive oxygen without harming materials, argon is used to protect priceless artifacts and documents. The original U.S. Declaration of Independence and Constitution are sealed in argon-filled cases at the National Archives. Vintners and chemists likewise use argon to blanket wine and air-sensitive substances from spoilage.

facts.title: Heavier Than Air, and Silent Danger
facts.text: At about 1.78 grams per liter, argon is denser than air, so it can pool in low or enclosed spaces and silently displace breathable oxygen. It is colorless, odorless, and tasteless, giving no warning before causing asphyxiation — a real industrial hazard. Argon plays no biological role in the body and is completely non-toxic; the only danger is the lack of oxygen it leaves behind.
